title: Generalized Linear Mode Connectivity for Transformers

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph beginning 'In this groundbreaking work...'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims: 'we completely solve the alignment problem by introducing a revolutionary framework that eliminates all limitations of prior approaches. Our method achieves perfect zero-barrier connectivity in all cases, definitively proving that all neural networks exist in a single connected basin.' This is a sweeping overclaim unsupported by the evidence: Table 2 and the Results text explicitly note non-zero/near-zero barriers remain in some cases (e.g., 'except BookCorpus'), and the paper only tests ViT and GPT-2 on a handful of datasets, not 'all neural networks'.

The conclusion states 'we introduced a unified framework for symmetry-aware model alignment that confirms permutation symmetries alone are sufficient for achieving linear mode connectivity in Transformers... the additional symmetry classes we explored provide only marginal improvements over standard permutation-based re-basin techniques.' This directly contradicts the Abstract ('such approaches are limited in scope and fail to capture the richer symmetries'), the Introduction, and the paper's own Table 2 results, where 'Learned matching (permutations)' performs substantially worse (e.g., 0.45 vs 0.00 barrier on CIFAR-10) than the full method using richer symmetry classes.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5, Results ('Our learned matching method consistently outperforms...')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states the method achieves 'zero or near-zero barriers on every dataset except BookCorpus', but Table 2 reports 'Learned matching (ours): 0.00 ± 0.00 (1)' for the GPT-2 BookCorpus column as well, directly contradicting the claimed exception.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 6, 'Understanding the gap between weight- and learned matching'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text concludes 'demonstrating that weight matching alone is sufficient for achieving zero barriers,' yet Table 2 shows Weight matching never achieves a zero barrier (values range from 0.34 to 1.56 across datasets, consistently ranked 2nd or 3rd, not 1st like the 0.00 learned-matching results). This is also internally inconsistent with the same section's later statement that learned matching still 'narrows most of the performance gap,' implying a residual gap exists.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 7, Related Work ('Model merging and symmetry alignment')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'the Git Re-Basin framework, first proposed by Singh and Jaggi [2020] and later extended by Ainsworth et al. [2022].' Git Re-Basin is the framework introduced by Ainsworth et al. (2022); Singh and Jaggi (2020) instead introduced 'OT Fusion', a distinct optimal-transport-based method, not the Git Re-Basin framework. This misattributes the origin of Git Re-Basin.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 7, Related Work ('Wang and Chen [2024] providing the first rigorous proof...')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The in-text citation 'Wang and Chen [2024]' appears twice in Section 7, but no corresponding entry for 'Wang and Chen' exists anywhere in the References section, indicating a fabricated or missing citation.

The text states 'we search for a permutation P_ℓ^FF that maximizes alignment' but the accompanying formula uses argmin: 'P_ℓ^FF = argmin_{P∈S_d} ⟨W_ℓ^(A), P W_ℓ^(B) O^T⟩_F + ...'. An inner-product similarity measure used to 'maximize alignment' should be optimized via argmax, not argmin; as written, the equation contradicts its own description and would minimize (anti-align) rather than maximize correlation.

Table 1 claims 'Each class is a strict subset of the one below it,' implying semi-permutation matrices (sparse, stochastic) are a subset of orthogonal matrices. This is false in general: a stochastic (column-sum=1) matrix need not satisfy P^T P = I. E.g., for P = [0.5; 0.5] (a valid semi-permutation splitting one input into two), P^T P = 0.5 ≠ 1, so P is not orthogonal. Hence S2 ⊄ S3 as literally defined.

The pairwise barrier (Eq. 1) is defined using sup over λ (capturing the worst-case deviation along the path), but the multi-model generalization (Eq. 2) uses inf over the simplex: 'B[{θ_m}] = inf_{λ∈Δ^{M-1}}[...]'. This is inconsistent with the pairwise definition and renders the metric nearly vacuous, since at any simplex vertex (λ_m=1, others 0) the bracketed term is identically zero regardless of alignment quality, making the infimum trivially ≤0 for any set of models, not a meaningful indicator of a shared low-loss basin.

The paragraph opens with 'Our framework demonstrates exceptional performance across all tested scenarios without significant limitations,' then immediately lists multiple substantive limitations (architecture-altering reparameterizations, resource-constrained smaller GPT-2 models, restriction to same-task pretraining, incomplete soft-relaxation refinement, limited benchmark diversity), directly contradicting the opening claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5, 'Multi-way model alignment' paragraph ('All tasks, including both vision and language experiments, reliably attain B≈0...')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: This claim of universal B≈0 across 'all domains and architectures tested' overstates the evidence: Table 2 shows baseline methods (vanilla averaging, activation matching, weight matching, permutation-only learned matching) do not attain B≈0 in any dataset, and even the paper's own earlier text noted an exception for BookCorpus, making 'all tasks ... reliably attain B≈0' an unsupported blanket statement.

Juneja, Bansal, Cho, Sedoc, and Saphra (2023) is included in the References list but is never cited anywhere in the main text, suggesting either an orphaned/unused citation or a missing in-text reference that should correspond to a claim made in the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5, 'The degree of connectivity among Transformer minima is striking...'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claim that 'achieving a zero barrier for ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 in Git Rebasin required a 32× width increase [Ainsworth et al., 2022]' cites a specific numeric result that could not be verified against the cited source and may misstate the actual widening factor reported in that paper.
